cards.definition: Electrostatic attraction between positively charged metal particles and delocalised electrons in a metallic lattice.
Electrons that are not attached to one particular atom and can move throughout a structure.
Bonding where attraction acts in all directions, allowing particles to shift while maintaining attraction.
Strong electrostatic attraction between positively charged cations and negatively charged anions.
A strong attraction formed when atoms share a pair of electrons.
A large continuous structure of atoms connected by strong covalent bonds.
A repeating three-dimensional arrangement of oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction.
A repeating structure of positive metal particles surrounded by delocalised electrons.
Attractive forces acting between separate molecules.
Attractive forces or bonds acting between atoms within the same particle or molecule.
The ability of a solid to be hammered, bent or moulded into a different shape without breaking.
The ability of a material to be drawn into a wire without breaking.
The tendency of a material to break or shatter when sufficient force is applied.
The ability of a substance to allow charged particles to move through it and carry electrical current.
The ability of a solute to dissolve in a solvent to form a solution.
Energy associated with the attractive forces holding oppositely charged ions together within an ionic lattice.
A molecule with an uneven distribution of charge, producing regions of partial positive and negative charge.
A separation of electrical charge that creates a partially positive region and a partially negative region.
Electrons in the outer shell of an atom that are involved in chemical bonding.
A pair of valence electrons located on an atom that is not involved in a covalent bond.
A region of electron density associated with a bond between atoms.
A region around an atom where negatively charged electrons are located.
The three-dimensional arrangement of atoms around a central atom in a molecule.
A molecular arrangement involving four bonding regions around a central atom, arranged for maximum separation.
A molecular shape involving three bonding regions and one lone pair around the central atom.
An organic compound made entirely from carbon and hydrogen atoms.
A hydrocarbon in which the carbon atoms have the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms attached.
A hydrocarbon containing a carbon-carbon double or triple bond and therefore not having the maximum possible hydrogen atoms.
A saturated hydrocarbon containing only single carbon-carbon bonds.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon triple bond.
A separation technique that separates components of a mixture according to differences in boiling point or volatility.
A measure of how readily a substance vaporises; more volatile substances enter the gas phase more easily.
A reaction where atoms are added across a multiple bond, producing a more saturated molecule.
A rule used to predict the major product when an unsymmetrical molecule is added across an unsymmetrical alkene.
The product formed in the greatest amount when a reaction can produce multiple structural products.
A possible product formed in a smaller amount than the major product.
A chemical reaction in which a fuel reacts with oxygen and releases energy.
Combustion occurring with sufficient oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water from the fuels considered in the exam.
Combustion occurring with limited oxygen, allowing products such as carbon monoxide and carbon to form.
A chemical reaction that releases energy to the surroundings.
The energy change associated with a chemical reaction; the exam uses a negative ΔH to indicate energy release.
The principle that matter is not created or destroyed during a chemical reaction.
A system in which matter cannot escape, allowing the total mass before and after a reaction to be compared.
A reaction in which two or more reactants combine to form one product.
A reaction in which one reactant breaks down to form two or more products.
A reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water.
A reaction involving soluble ionic substances that produces an insoluble solid.
An insoluble solid formed from substances reacting in solution.
A substance capable of donating hydrogen ions, H⁺, and producing a conjugate base.
An acid that fully dissociates into ions in solution.
An acid that only partially dissociates, establishing an equilibrium between ionised and unionised forms.
The process in which a substance separates into ions when in solution.
The species remaining after an acid has donated a hydrogen ion.
A condition in which forward and reverse processes occur, represented in the exam using a reversible arrow.
An acid capable of donating two hydrogen ions.
The lowering of ocean pH associated in the exam with CO₂ reacting with seawater and increasing acidity.
A measure related in the exam to the number of successful particle collisions occurring each second.
The amount of time required for a reaction to reach completion.
The idea that reacting particles must collide with sufficient energy and an appropriate orientation for a successful reaction.
A collision between reactant particles that has sufficient energy and suitable orientation to produce a reaction.
The minimum energy requirement that must be overcome for a chemical reaction to occur.
A substance that increases reaction rate by providing a pathway with a lower activation energy.
The amount of a substance present within a particular volume of solution.
The amount of a solid reactant exposed and available for collisions with other reactant particles.
A different structural form of the same chemical element in the same physical state.
A carbon allotrope consisting of covalently bonded layers with delocalised electrons and weaker attractions between layers.
A carbon allotrope consisting of a three-dimensional network of carbon atoms connected by strong covalent bonds.
A large molecule made from many smaller repeating units linked together in long chains.
A smaller molecule capable of joining with other monomers to form a polymer.
A chemical reaction in which monomers join together to form a polymer.
The structural section of a polymer that repeats throughout the polymer chain.
A manufactured polymer, such as polyethylene, Kevlar or nylon in the exam classification.
A naturally occurring polymer, such as DNA, silk or collagen in the exam classification.
